subject: Use of "colour" etc. with integer variables

messages.author: 473c4ce8ca8f75f2
messages.subject: Use of "colour" etc. with integer variables
parts:
Hello again

On p. 45 of the book there is this code


p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt, colour = cyl)) + geom_point()
p


which produces a graph with a legend including cylinders = 5 and 7. But no
dots for those, although it's a bit hard to tell that there are none. Still,
while I am not a car buff, I've never heard of a 5 or 7 cylinder car.

table(mtcars$cyl)

reveals that, sure enough, there are only 4, 6, and 8 cylinder cars.

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt, colour = as.factor(cyl))) + geom_point()
p

produces a plot with only three colors of dots, but in the order 6, 4, 8 ...
perhaps reverse alphabetical order? It is much easier to distinguish these colors
than the ones produced by what is in the book.

I thought of

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt, colour = as.ordered(cyl))) + geom_point()
p

but this produces the same as the as.factor code.

Looking at the chapter on legends, I tried

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt, colour = as.factor(cyl))) + geom_point() + scale_x_discrete()
p


So, I am learning how to find solutions, which makes me happy and may cut down on my beginner-type posts to the
list :-), but shouldn't this be easier to do? I would even think it might be the default to not have
colors assigned to levels that do not exist.

Or am I, as usual, missing something?

Peter


this produces an error

Error in unit(at, "native") : 'x' and 'units' must have length > 0


which is not clear, at least not to me.

but then I found the solution

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt, colour = as.factor(cyl))) + geom_point() + scale_colour_hue(breaks = c(4,6,8))
p

messages.author: cb25d91fd630a4e5
messages.subject: Re: Use of "colour" etc. with integer variables
parts:
When a continuous variable is supplied as a mapping to colour, a
continuous colour scale is used. When a categorical (factored)
variable is supplied as a mapping to colour, a discrete colour scale
is used.

These are reasonable/useful defaults and put the onus on the user to
know the structure of their data.

Similarly, ggplot plots categorical (factored) variables in the order
that they are leveled in the original data. Look at the relev()
command in the package "ez" for a simple way of re-ordering the levels
of a factor (if you look at the source, it simply loops relevel() ).

> p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt, colour = as.factor(cyl))) + geom_point()
> p
>
> produces a plot with only three colors of dots, but in the order 6, 4, 8 ...

I don't replicate your observation that the order is 6,4,8; using
ggplot 0.8.3 I observe the expected order of 4,6,8.
